If my lion father supports me,
I shall begin the holy war in earnest!
Against the grim Black Chinese,
I shall enter directly and scout the road;
For my godfather Almambet,
I shall at last take revenge.
My godfather Almambet—
All twelve parts of our bodies were alike;
Your gray wolf gone to the next world
Was a lion born as my true brother.
Against the teeming infidels,
When he unleashed utter turmoil,
That restless, unruly faith—
He was the lion who opened its gate;
Of the surging Black Chinese,
He was the hero who broke their host.
If I do not gird my waist for hardship,
If I do not cry aloud and seek
The blood-price of my blessed godfather,
If I do not bring slaughter upon the world,
From Chinese as numerous as ants
If I do not take Almambet's blood-price!”
When Semetey said this,
Bakai stood and answered:
“Ah, my foal, Semetey,
If you enter Beijing, there are many roads;
If we take plunder, that too is abundant.
If we slaughter them and take revenge,
The blood-price is enough to be remembered for an age.
There are many black, low hills and cliffs,
And many enemies to grapple.
To your left are the Chinese,
And many foes to fight.
To your right are the Russians;
Before you are firearms,
And many foes to oppose.
There are pits dug and waiting,
And roads upon which to grapple.
There are many costly passes to cross,
And many heroes lying in ambush.
There are many horses to ride on holy war;
My foal, my son Semetey,
If I keep speaking, there are many grievances.
If you set your face toward China,
My wise one who will bring slaughter,
If you campaign against the infidels,
What will you do, my son Semetey?
You have only now become blood-footed;
Your soul has not yet found rest,
And your blood has not reached full strength!
Without grieving your uncle Bakai,
Heed him this year.
Without grieving your uncle Bakai,
Go in the coming year!
Carefully scout the road
To Beijing beyond a saint's reach.
If you wage holy war against Kakan-Chyn,
The Chinese are numerous as black worms.
Against infidels like black worms,
You have chosen to grapple;
Against hero Khan Kongurbai,
He is no foe to rush upon thoughtlessly.
Sacred Great Beijing—
None who grapple it returns unharmed.
From radiance-pouring Beijing,
Of Beijing's forty gates,
I have seen one gate.
Closed by day, by day it stood open;
Its mouth opened toward the qibla.
At the mouth of that gate,
The Bismillah verse was written.
The followers of Muhammad—
When they came into Muslim hands,
Lest a devil strike them,
God's light was scattered there.
They have pride, but no faith;
That is the land pouring forth radiance.
I am that battered Bakai
Who devoured its great lords!
Let us reckon the years,
And choose an auspicious year
To go to mourning Beijing!
Let us reckon the days,
Set the day down in writing,
And choose an auspicious day
To go to lowering Beijing!
The Kakanchin have their people
And giants of many kinds;
By custom they drink the blood
Of the mortal who challenges them.
Chin-Machin has its people,
And the true Kalcha has eyes;
Its people swarm in multitudes,
And by custom drink the blood
Of those who go against them.
Yesterday, when Saint Ali the lion
Went there intending to fight,
When he brought splendid slaughter,
When he went intending to destroy them
And unleashed great turmoil,
When he was about to convert
The defeated Chinese to Islam,
A voice sounded from heaven
And appeared to Ali the lion:
"There is abundance and no hunger;
This Beijing surges with people.
In heaven Chalyiar's voice rang out;
It has no faith, but it has number.
Carpets lie spread across the land;
Great Beijing is bathed in radiance.
Turn back without troubling yourself."
When he heard this voice,
Saint Ali turned away;
Without fighting Beijing,
He turned back midway.
That is a land from which none return;
Those Chinese are a prolific people,
Smoldering anew whenever they are depleted,
Rooting themselves and growing ever stronger—
A people upon whom a prayer remains!
They multiply whenever they die;
Those are the ruling Chinese people.
The Almighty himself chose it;
That is a land blessed with abundance!
Do not behave recklessly,
Saying you will set your face
Toward fortified Beijing!
Yesterday, in Kakanchin's Beijing,
Its Kalmaks swarmed;
When God scattered their seed,
They covered the face of the earth.
From sunrise to sunset,
They are a multitude made of men,
A teeming Chinese people.
Kara Khan, father of the people,
Was of Kyrgyz stock.
He met his death and died;
When Kara Khan's eight sons
Were left young and crawling,
The Chinese seized them
And divided them by the lash;
Those fated to die perished.
They drove one away to Eren
And cast him into the deep.
They drove one to Altai,
And another to Kangai.
The eight were scattered,
Some of them twins born of one mother;
Unable to find them by asking everywhere,
How many souls withered away.
That Yakyp was driven away,
And Manas was born in Altai.
When he heard of his kinsmen's fate,
Your falcon father, the leopard,
Born there in Altai,
Threw China into turmoil.
Your bloodthirsty father, the leopard,
Unleashed the upheaval;
Esen Khan was a great lord,
But your father brought him hardship then
And slaughtered him utterly.
People fell into ruin on hearing his name;
The calamities your father wrought
Were inscribed in the register
Of the khan of Kakanchin.
Yesterday, at Kökötöi's feast,
An evil quarrel arose from the Chinese,
And many disputes arose from the Kyrgyz.
The twelve Muslim khans,
Along the broad Alai,
At hero Töshtük's feast,
Said, "We shall plunder the Bloodthirsty One
And bring an upheaval!"
They sent envoys,
Stirring up the ancient madness;
After rousing the Muslims
To charge and make war
Against Kakanchin's Beijing,
They said they would enter directly
Into lowering great Beijing and level their spears.
The road was blessed by Khizr,
And the army numbered forty-two tumens.
All the saints were there,
And all twelve Muslim khans
Were among them.
They had wrestlers and a great people;
All their heroes were there.
They had skillful spearmen,
And champions who knew the enemy's stratagems.
There were lions Almambet and Chubak,
And leopards Serek and Syrgak,
Heroes who had traversed the world.
They stood against the enemy
And fought without pause for six months,
Remaining there without pause for six months.
When they were exacting judgment
From Beijing, where even Solomon had not gone,
Swaggering heroes died,
Many generous souls died,
And everyone who met the foe died.
When they turned back this way,
Beijing's affairs recovered,
And all the valiant men were lost.
Great Beijing is a place from which none return;
It shears down everyone from the head.
Every living soul who went there died;
Many khans died.
Do not ask what Beijing is like:
Its passes are said to be dug trenches,
And its road one from which none return.
Whoever sets his face toward it is killed;
Great Beijing's danger is fierce.
Whoever goes there does not turn back;
Whoever meets it does not return alive.
Many people have gone
To Kakanchin's Beijing,
But none have come back.
It yielded no judgment to Suuk Kol,
And even Zulqarnain did not go there.
The road to Beijing has five branches,
Bringing peril upon the wretched head.
Beijing is no empty land,
Nor are its people to be approached lightly.
One road to Beijing
Is a road from which none return;
One road to Beijing
Has a deep-dug trench;
One road to Beijing
Has suffering set boiling;
On one road to Beijing,
Whoever meets it does not escape alive;
On one road to Beijing,
Whoever meets it does not return alive.
Beijing is that prolific land,
And the Chinese that mighty people.
My worthy one, I am Bakai,
Who knows all that can be known."
When Bakai finished speaking,
Your dear mother Kanykei—
From her dear quail-like eyes,
Tears fell one after another;
From her dear currant-black eyes,
Tears streamed a whip's length.
Her heart was torn apart,
And tears poured from her eyes;
Allah's sun in the sky grew overcast,
And sixty cares came upon her head:
The dear bird called the kazgaldak
Flies without turning back in search of food;
How much this wretched head has endured
For you who came from my womb.
The dear bird called the bezbeldek
Flies crying shrilly in search of food;
How much toil I, poor woman, have borne
For you who came from my body.
